newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank's Welteke sees EMU debt goal flexibility.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank's Welteke sees EMU debt goal flexibility.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke was quoted on Sunday as saying that the Maastricht Treaty allowed for flexibility on the budgetary goals countries must reach to take part in the planned euro launch in 1999.

In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung newspaper, Welteke said the overall political situation would be taken into account when judging which countries qualify to start the European Union's common currency.

Asked what significance the Maastricht criteria would have in next year's selection process, Welteke, a supporter of the euro, replied: "Totally strict adherence to the numerically defined goals for inflation, interest rates and exchange rates and use of interpretative leeway on the fiscal criterion."
Alongside other demands, Maastricht calls on countries not to allow their 1997 budget deficits exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) or their total debt to exceed 60 percent of GDP.

The level of flexibility on these criteria has become a hot issue in recent months amid concern that Germany will struggle to meet these thresholds this year with its current record unemployment levels.

Welteke said the Maastricht Treaty made no direct reference to what would happen if a country failed to meet the budgetary goals. "But nonetheless the fiscal criterion is described in such a way that the overall political situation is also taken into account," he said.
Welteke added that this flexibility made economic sense since rising debt was not necessarily inflationary.
"The connection between public debt and stability is actually not that great: For example we will probably have an inflation rate of 1.5 percent this month, alongside rising public debt."
The central banker also criticised politicians for failing to devote enough energy to convincing the sceptical German public that the single currency project was a good idea.
"It is a question now of taking away people's fear that they will suffer a loss of wealth or buying power under currency union. There is no basis for this," he said.

However he said the German state was right to decide to postpone switching its own finances to the euro until euros are available in cash, from 2002. Pension payments in euros, for example, would be meaningless before that time.

He also said he expected Bonn to opt to convert its existing government debt issues to euros from January 1 1999, a move viewed by many as crucial for the future competitive position of German capital markets.
Turning to the economy, Welteke agreed that a higher inflation rate might help the German debt situation by boosting GDP.
But asked if the Bundesbank would have to take steps to control the situation should inflation accelerate, Welteke said: "We will be on guard."
